facts.text: The laughing kookaburra is the largest kingfisher in the world, even outweighing the giant kingfisher.
facts.quote: The laughing kookaburra is the largest species of kingfisher, outsizing even the giant kingfisher in body mass.

facts.text: It is a stocky bird 41–47 cm long with a white head, a dark brown stripe across each eye and a long, robust bill.
facts.quote: It is a stout, stocky bird 41–47 cm (16–19 in) in length, with a large head, prominent brown eyes, and a long and robust bill.

facts.text: Its famous laugh is used to mark territory and is most often heard at dawn and dusk.
facts.quote: the bird's "laugh", which it uses to establish territory among family groups. It can be heard at any time of day, but most frequently at dawn and dusk.

facts.text: The female lays three white eggs at about two-day intervals, incubated by both parents and helper birds for 24–26 days.
facts.quote: The female generally lays a clutch of three semi-glossy, white, rounded eggs, measuring 36 mm × 45 mm (1.4 in × 1.8 in), at about two-day intervals. Both parents and auxiliaries incubate the eggs for 24–26 days.

facts.text: When food is scarce, chicks use a hook on the bill as a weapon and the smallest may be killed by its siblings.
facts.quote: If the food supply to the chicks is not adequate, the chicks will quarrel, with the hook being used as a weapon. The smallest chick may even be killed by its larger siblings.

facts.text: It is monogamous and lives in family groups, with up to five grown offspring helping parents defend territory and raise young.
facts.quote: A breeding pair can be accompanied by up to five fully grown non-breeding offspring from previous years that help the parents defend their territory and raise their young.

facts.text: It typically waits perched on a branch until it sees an animal on the ground, then flies down and pounces on its prey.
facts.quote: A predator of a wide variety of small animals, the laughing kookaburra typically waits perched on a branch until it sees an animal on the ground and then flies down and pounces on its prey.

facts.text: It is known to take goldfish out of garden ponds.
facts.quote: Its diet includes lizards, insects, worms, snakes, mice and it is known to take goldfish out of garden ponds.

facts.text: Kookaburras sometimes take large creatures, including venomous snakes, much longer than their bodies.
facts.quote: Small prey are preferred, but kookaburras sometimes take large creatures, including venomous snakes, much longer than their bodies.

facts.text: The kookaburra's song is a learned behavior, though the structure for producing calls is present from an early age.
facts.quote: While the structure for producing calls is present from an early age, the kookaburra's song is a learned behavior.
